Sports.summary: It is as if Harry Kane cannot get enough of tormenting Arsenal. The Bayern Munich striker has plenty of form from his Tottenham days. He remains the top scorer in north London derby history with 14 goals. He made an impact yet again here and yet it was not a night when he had the final word. That honour fell to Declan Rice, the Arsenal midfielder storming into the Bayern area in the 82nd minute to guide home a low finish that Kane would have been proud to call his own. Arsenal were hunting their latest statement result. Only once had they ever won away against Bayern – the 2-0 in the Champions League last 16 second leg in 2013, although it did not prevent an away goals exit. Mikel Arteta was an Arsenal player that night. When Eberechi Eze, who came on for the injured Bukayo Saka in the 10th minute, gave them the lead midway through the first half, their hopes surged. Culture.title: Ilford Boy review – Barbra Streisand teaches teen to smile about the way we are
Culture.summary: Donmar Warehouse, London In Danny Lee Wynter’s drama, a quiet boy struggles amid the swirl of his family until a mercurial friend offers him another future Broad Essex accents fill the stage in Danny Lee Wynter’s sprawling family drama. The busy script from the Black Superhero playwright is crammed with a fractious extended family treading heavily over old arguments, but the production sings when an old friend swans back into town. Set across the 80s and 90s in the shadow of the Aids crisis, this story’s beating heart travels around on tap shoes. Quiet teenager Ted (Leo Whitfield Harris in his stage debut) is surrounded by the loud swirl of his feuding family, with everyone’s rusty views on queerness, race and masculinity grating against each other as they clear out his showtune-loving nanna’s house in Ilford. His father (a bolshie Gershwyn Eustache Jr) is pushing him towards boxing and girls, so Ted grits his teeth and resists anything seen as weakness, but in doing so he resists kindness too. Culture.title: Perle Noire: Meditations for Joséphine review – turgid tribute to pioneering star
Culture.summary: Barbican Hall, London Julia Bullock is magnetic in this discourse on Josephine Baker, but the 100-minute piece is slow-moving and lacking in intimacy Josephine Baker was many things: a civil rights activist; a spy for the French resistance; a woman who, born into poverty, became the best-paid stage star in Europe. But before she was any of these, she was an entertainer. So one wonders what on earth she would make of Perle Noire: Meditations for Joséphine, a turgid 100-minute piece developed by the soprano Julia Bullock, composer Tyshawn Sorey, poet Claudia Rankine and director Peter Sellars. This was its UK premiere, although Bullock and Sorey have been performing versions of it in the US and elsewhere over the past decade. It isn’t a tribute in the usual sense, but a discourse on racial discrimination, in Baker’s day and our own. Bullock, magnetic as ever, sings and speaks alongside six musicians, who include Sorey himself on piano, drum kit and percussion, plus electric guitar, violin, alto flute, saxophone and bassoon. On a platform, in front of a saturated square of brightly coloured light, Bullock declaims Rankine’s words and sings Sorey’s music, in which Baker’s songs are deconstructed, reformed, and mostly slowed right down. A riff on Bye Bye Blackbird has guitar and saxophone sounding suspiciously like the playout on a 1980s power ballad. Later, more rewardingly, the guitar gives a highlife flavour to a version of Je t’aime. But mostly the score is bloated and the instrumental episodes don’t unify the piece so much as draw it out. Ear-splitting bass drum and tam tam indicate emotional climaxes. Everyone is mic’d up, which works against any sense of intimacy. Continue reading...
